summary: The Remote Job Entry protocol, written by Bressler, Guida and McKenzie, for sending batch jobs to a remote server. A user controls the server over a Telnet connection to a special logger, and the server uses FTP to fetch the job input and deliver the output. It obsoletes RFC 360. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Remote Job Entry lets a user ask another host to run a batch job. The user controls the work over Telnet, while the server uses FTP to move input and output files.

subtitle: How users submitted batch jobs to remote hosts and received their output.

tldr.problem: A user needed a standard way to submit a batch-processing job to a remote host and receive its output.
tldr.mechanism: The user sends commands over Telnet to an RJE Logger; the server uses FTP to retrieve input files and deliver output files.
tldr.outcome: RFC 407 obsoletes RFC 360 and has Historic status.

sections.title: How Remote Job Entry Works
sections.content:
Remote job entry (RJE) lets a person or process at one site request that a remote batch-processing server run a job. The server retrieves a job-input file, processes it and delivers output files to a remote location.

The user sends control commands over a Telnet connection to the RJE Logger at socket 5, not socket 1. The server uses File Transfer Protocol (FTP) to retrieve input and deliver output. Commands and replies are designed to be understood by people and user processes.
sections.plainLanguage: A user sends control commands to an RJE server over Telnet. The server fetches the job file with FTP, runs it and transfers the results.

sections.title: Commands and Output Choices
sections.content:
Commands are sent one per line. The first command on a new Telnet connection is USER, followed by a password command when needed. Other commands identify input and output files, start input, request job status, cancel or alter a job, or end the connection.

The OUT command chooses whether an output file is transferred and discarded, held without transfer, or transferred and saved. CHANGE can alter a job's output disposition. Certain NET control cards at the start of an input file can set output options for that job and take precedence over matching Telnet commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The user identifies the job's input and chooses where its output should go. The protocol also includes commands to check, cancel or change a job.

sections.title: Moving Job Files with FTP
sections.content:
Most files that do not use TIP devices are transferred through FTP. The RJE server calls its local FTP user, which connects to the FTP server at the other host. The protocol describes choices for data coding and transfer format, and uses separate FTP connections for individual files.

For output, the server can send restart markers. If a transfer is incomplete and the output was set to transmit and save, the user may use RECOVER to restart from the last remembered marker. The memo also describes how the server handles failed transfers and inaccessible destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP moves each job file between hosts. Restart markers can let a saved output transfer resume after an interruption.

sections.title: Numbered Replies and Job Examples
sections.content:
Each server action and Telnet command receives a reply consisting of a three-digit code, a blank and explanatory text. The first digit identifies the response type, the second identifies its general subject, and the third gives a more specific meaning. For example, 200 acknowledges a command, 230 reports completed log-on and 260 reports that a job was accepted for processing.

The RFC provides command-reply tables and example sequences for TIP users and users who run a job at one host with input from another. The examples show the control exchange and the server's file transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: The server answers commands with a code and text. Programs can use the code to identify the result, while people can read the explanation.
